look_here_first: RED FLOWERS ARE NOT THE ID. Start with the LEAVES: scarlet sage has many broad triangular-to-ovate SIMPLE leaves on prominent petioles up an upright, branching stem, not a cedar-sage basal rosette nor big-red-sage's large thick smooth basal leaves. Check the interrupted flower spike and calyces next; wild flowers are often red but cultivated selections can also be pink/white.

key_traits.label: Habit
key_traits.text: Annual to short-lived perennial/subshrub tendency; usually branched, often 0.5–1 m tall.

key_traits.label: Leaves
key_traits.text: Opposite decussate, simple, petiolate; blades triangular or ovate to deltoid with serrate margins.

key_traits.label: Inflorescence
key_traits.text: Interrupted series of verticils/cymes along a terminal axis.

key_traits.label: Calyx
key_traits.text: Persistent, ribbed and enlarging around developing nutlets.

key_traits.label: Floral detail
key_traits.text: Long bilateral corolla; typically red in local material but color is secondary to leaf and inflorescence structure.

key_traits.label: Life cycle
key_traits.text: Annual or short-lived perennial depending on frost and site, herbaceous branched upper stems; an open, weedlike shoot is supportive but not sole proof.

key_traits.label: Leaf diagnostic
key_traits.text: Simple (one undivided blade), opposite broad ovate/deltoid, petiolate with serrate edges; no lateral leaflets as on some cedar sage leaves.

key_traits.label: Flower arrangement
key_traits.text: Red tubular two-lipped corollas in separate spaced flowering whorls on branched/terminal upright spikes; persistent calyces remain after petals fall.

key_traits.label: Compare roemeriana
key_traits.text: Cedar sage is a taprooted perennial with conspicuous basal rosette and leaves sometimes 1–3-foliolate on long petioles. Its calyx is ~11 mm (UT), and flower spikes usually arise from a woodland leaf rosette.

key_traits.label: Compare pentstemonoides
key_traits.text: Big red sage has thick, smooth, large basal rosette leaves (to ~12 cm) and flowers about 4 cm, on tall stalks (to ~1.5 m), usually seep-fed limestone ravines; FWS source.
